html:
The Lapita were Austronesian seafarers who settled the islands of the western Pacific between about 1600 and 500 BCE, from the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea out to Tonga and Samoa. They are the direct ancestors of the Polynesians.

They are known mainly by their pottery, stamped with fine toothed tools in geometric patterns and sometimes faces. The style closely matches pottery from northern Luzon, which fits the idea that they came from the Philippines after the Austronesian move south from Taiwan, directly or by way of the Mariana Islands.

What stands out:

  • Speed. Within a few centuries they crossed from the Bismarcks to Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, a jump of thousands of kilometres of open sea, much of it to islands no human had ever reached.
  • Packing for settlement. They carried pigs, dogs, chickens, taro, yams and breadfruit with them.
  • Exchange. Obsidian from the Bismarcks turns up far away, a sign that islands stayed in touch.
  • Mixing. In Melanesia they married into older Papuan-speaking populations.

After about 500 BCE the decorated pottery fades out. In Tonga and Samoa a new culture grew from Lapita roots over the next thousand years: ancestral Polynesian society. From there later voyagers carried out the settlement of East Polynesia, and Tonga became the base of the Tuʻi Tonga.
sum: The Lapita were Austronesian seafarers who settled the islands of the western Pacific between about 1600 and 500 BCE, from the Bismarck Archipelago off New Guinea out to Tonga and Samoa. They are the direct ancestors of the Polynesians.
